summary: Steel-company breakwater light at Gary, Indiana, first lit in 1911; a steel tower on a private U.S. Steel pier, tower closed.

structures.type: steel cylindrical tower on a concrete base
structures.note: About 30 ft (9 m) tall (LighthouseFriends). Terry Pepper describes a stepped cylindrical tower with a lantern.

access.note: Private industrial pier owned by U.S. Steel. Tower closed; LighthouseFriends advises viewing from the water.

events.note: New steel tower on a concrete base at the outer end of the breakwater; breakwater built over 1910 and 1911
Exhibited for the first time on the night of 5 July 1911
Fog siren established at the lighthouse 3 October 1913 (LighthouseFriends); Terry Pepper describes a siren with the 1911 structure; see resolved_conflicts
Sy Meredith, a U.S. Steel electrician, trapped at the light in a storm on 7 April 1914 and taken off by the South Chicago Lifesaving Station; LighthouseFriends' account, which gives no source
Taken off the breakwater for sandblasting, repair and repainting

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends and Terry Pepper both give the first lighting as the night of 5 July 1911. The 1913 date matches the fog siren that LighthouseFriends dates to 3 October 1913, which may be the source of the USLHS year (an inference, not a source's statement).
The tower was built with the breakwater over 1910 and 1911 and first exhibited in July 1911.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS archive gives 1913 as year established and year tower established. LighthouseFriends and Terry Pepper give 5 July 1911. The 1913 date appears to be the fog signal; see corrections.

The 1911 signal is described two ways: LighthouseFriends gives two white flashes every four seconds, Terry Pepper a 15.7 second group of two flashes. The present group flashing red every forty seconds (LighthouseFriends) agrees with the recorded Fl(3) R 40s.

The record gives a concrete crib (USLHS foundation). LighthouseFriends and Terry Pepper describe a steel tower on a concrete base at the end of a stone-filled timber crib breakwater, so the crib is the breakwater, not the tower.

Terry Pepper describes a six-inch air-operated siren as part of the 1911 structure (2-second blast, 28 seconds silence). LighthouseFriends dates the fog siren (a Scotch siren, air from a compressor on shore) to 3 October 1913. The record gives no fog-signal date. The story states both accounts and does not choose between them.

The USLHS archive lists the station as 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No'. LighthouseFriends gives the present signal (group flashing red every forty seconds) and a horn that sounds when needed; Terry Pepper (page last modified 2012) says ships still look for the light. The story states the conflict and does not settle it; the USCG list is still to be checked.

sources.title: Seeing The Light: Gary Breakwater Lighthouse

notes_for_editor: Thin-to-moderate station: three web sources, none primary. No keeper is named for the light in any source used; the USLHS roster is empty and the Lighthouse Service reports (corpus, 1891-1939) carry no entry for it, consistent with a light run by the steel company. The 1914 rescue comes only from LighthouseFriends, which gives no source; I searched Chronicling America for April 1914 in Indiana and nationally for Meredith and breakwater and found nothing. The 1910 hearings are as Terry Pepper summarises them (his reference is the 1910 River and Harbor report, not read). The U.S. Coast Guard Historian's Gary page could not be read: the live site is blocked, and both Internet Archive captures I tried returned 403 or 404. The Coast Guard Historic Light Station PDF on media.defense.gov was also refused (403). Status: the record says inactive, the USLHS says active aid to navigation no, but Terry Pepper (2012) says ships still look for the light and LighthouseFriends says the horn sounds when needed. Confirm the current status against the USCG list (LLNR 7-19610) before publishing. Position: the OSM point (41.630379, -87.320332) agrees with Terry Pepper's GPS (about 41.63033, -87.32029); the USLHS position (41.6248, -87.3188) is about 0.6 km away. The Lake County Times (Hammond) is in Chronicling America for 1909-1913 and may hold local coverage of the 1911 lighting; several searches and three page reads (Lake County Times, 1909-1913) found nothing about the light itself. Access: the USLHS and LighthouseFriends agree the tower is closed; I did not confirm whether the breakwater can be reached by boat.
